As therapists exploring the profound depths of grief, we understand its layers. Some are evident, yet others we may not even recognize. The grieving process feels immediate as if it is happening right now, and distant, as though it occurred long ago. It continuously redraws its neural map, seeking to reinterpret and reinvent life without a loved one—or something that was once alive and vibrant in our world but is now absent. When someone or something is alive with us, it fortifies that connection. The spiritual mind yearns to believe that these lives are eternal. The smoke rises like a whisper unanswered, curling through the morning air with the patience of all forgotten prayers, and I think of the old archivist in her room, bent over recording equipment that glows with tiny red lights—each one a small beacon against the coming darkness. She's mapping the city's sounds before the dust storms arrive, catching birdsong and traffic hum, the particular way metal expands in heat, the last conversations of people who don't yet know they're saying goodbye. Everything will be buried in silt, she knows—every familiar echo, every routine noise we've stopped noticing—but still she works, her steady hands transcribing what remains, fingers moving across controls with the muscle memory of decades. This is determination, perhaps, or something more primal
